name: Vilenkin-Gott Cosmic String
description: The conical spacetime around an infinitely thin, straight topological defect, locally flat but with an angular deficit set by the string's tension. It produces no local gravity yet causes global lensing and double images.
history: Tom Kibble spent the middle of the 1970s asking what a cooling universe does with a symmetry it can no longer afford, and answered in 1976 that the vacuum will not agree with itself. Along certain lines the old symmetric phase stays trapped, held by the topology of the manifold of degenerate vacua rather than by anything local [kibble1976]. What is left is a thread thinner than a proton drawn across cosmological distances, its tension equal to its mass per unit length.¶To the space around it the thread does almost nothing, which is the surprise. Alexander Vilenkin computed the field of a straight string in linearized gravity in 1981 and found that space flat, the whole gravitational effect packed into a deficit angle fixed by the tension [vilenkin1981]. Set a test particle down beside a cosmic string and it stays where you put it. The geometry is still not Minkowski: a wedge has been cut from every plane the string crosses and the edges sewn together, leaving a cone. J. Richard Gott gave the exact solution in 1985, that cone outside and a spherical cap within, and read the optics off it [gott1985]. The missing wedge lenses by itself, so one quasar behind the string shows up twice at equal brightness and the microwave sky steps in temperature across its track.¶Those signatures made strings a candidate engine for cosmic structure. Robert Brandenberger and Neil Turok computed in 1986 what a network of them would stamp on the microwave background [brandenberger1986], and Brandenberger's 1994 review set out the defect theory and the tests that would settle it [brandenberger1994]. They settled it against: strings do not drive the primordial plasma in step, and the acoustic peaks later measured so cleanly are the sound of something that does.¶Then Gott came back to his own solution and used it to break time. His 1991 paper gives the exact geometry of two straight strings passing one another without touching, and shows that once each moves fast enough in the laboratory frame, a traveler who loops around both while they pass returns to his own past [gott1991]. The threshold is explicit: each string's Lorentz factor must exceed $1/\sin(4\pi\mu)$, where $8\pi\mu$ is the deficit angle it carries. Neither string misbehaves. Each alone is the harmless cone of 1985, and a circuit of either one brings you home late, never early. Curt Cutler mapped the global structure the year after, penning the closed curves into a bounded region that grows out of complete spacelike surfaces carrying none [cutler1992]. It was starting to look less like a pathology and more like a machine.¶A deficit angle is a global fact, and that is the whole trick: nothing near a string betrays it, and only a trip the whole way around turns the missing wedge up in the total. So a ship circling the pair can beat a light signal sent through the flat space between them, and while the strings are moving it beats it in time as well.¶The objections came fast. Stanley Deser, Roman Jackiw and Gerard 't Hooft, who had made gravity in three dimensions a flat space problem in 1984 [deser1984], added up the energy and momentum of Gott's pair and found it tachyonic: together the strings move faster than light though neither does alone, so the pair cannot be realized by physical, timelike sources [deser1992]. Four pages earlier in that same Physical Review Letters, Sean Carroll, Edward Farhi and Alan Guth built the spacetime of one gravitating particle decaying into two and found that an open universe never holds enough energy to push the products up to Gott's threshold [carroll1992]. A closed universe will let you assemble the pair, and 't Hooft shut that door too: such a universe has a finite lifetime and crunches before anybody finishes the circuit [thooft1992]. Amos Ori had come at it earlier still, showing that if such a spacetime has closed curves at all, every surface of constant time in it meets one, so the machine was never switched on [ori1991].¶Hawking generalized the quarrel in 1992. Causality violation growing in a finite region out of an infinite initial surface must break the averaged weak energy condition on its Cauchy horizon, which disposes of closed curves made from finite lengths of string; and as a curve nears closure the expectation value of the stress tensor runs away, wrecking the horizon before any traveler arrives [hawking1992]. There is, he wrote, "a Chronology Protection Agency which prevents the appearance of closed timelike curves and so makes the universe safe for historians." Manufacture is what is ruled out; chronology protection is still a conjecture, since the divergence it leans on arrives where the semiclassical approximation gives out [visser2003]. Gott's spacetime is still there, an exact solution made of two threads of positive energy obeying every energy condition, with no wormhole, no exotic matter and no singularity in it. That is why an argument about time travel so often ends up back at two cosmic strings.
